course_title: Practical Exercise on European and Global Legal History
title: Exercise class 8: constitutionalism, the Rechtsstaat, fundamental rights

slides.title: What the age of modern constitutions rests on
slides.text: THE AGE OF MODERN CONSTITUTIONS BEGINS WITH THE AMERICAN (1776) AND FRENCH (1789) REVOLUTIONS, and the exercise class lists SIX PILLARS on which both stood: (1) ENLIGHTENMENT NATURAL-LAW THINKING; (2) THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE; (3) LIMITED GOVERNMENT; (4) FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS FOR ALL CITIZENS; (5) THE SEPARATION OF POWERS; (6) THE RULE OF LAW. This six-part list is worth knowing by heart, because it is a ready-made skeleton for any question about constitutionalism. THE SPREAD: THE FRENCH REVOLUTION HAD A STRONG INFLUENCE ON PEOPLE ALL OVER EUROPE, and the same holds for the FRENCH CONSTITUTION OF 1791. And the driving force was not ideas alone: THE IDEAS OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION WERE SPREAD ACROSS EUROPE BY THE FRENCH REVOLUTIONARY AND NAPOLEONIC WARS (1792–1815). Constitutionalism therefore travelled with the army as much as with books.

cards.q: On which six pillars does the age of modern constitutions rest?
cards.a: 1) ENLIGHTENMENT NATURAL-LAW THINKING. 2) THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE. 3) LIMITED GOVERNMENT. 4) FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS FOR ALL CITIZENS. 5) THE SEPARATION OF POWERS. 6) THE RULE OF LAW. The age begins with the AMERICAN (1776) AND FRENCH (1789) REVOLUTIONS.

cards.q: What was the driving force behind the spread of constitutional ideas across Europe?
cards.a: Besides the influence of the French Revolution and the CONSTITUTION OF 1791, above all the FRENCH REVOLUTIONARY AND NAPOLEONIC WARS (1792–1815) — constitutionalism therefore travelled WITH THE ARMY as much as with books.

slides.title: The Pillersdorf Constitution: what exactly it introduced and whom it did not cover
slides.text: For April 1848 the exercise class gives details that come in useful in the exam. UNDER THE PRESSURE OF EVENTS — THE MARCH REVOLUTION — THE RULERS OF AUSTRIA AND PRUSSIA PROMISED CONSTITUTIONS IN THE SPRING OF 1848. ON 25 APRIL 1848 AUSTRIA RECEIVED ITS FIRST CONSTITUTION IN THE FORMAL SENSE, the Pillersdorf Constitution, WHICH TURNED CISLEITHANIA INTO A CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY. AND AN IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION: LOMBARDY-VENETIA AND HUNGARY WERE EXCLUDED FROM ITS SCOPE. The constitution is a typical example of EARLY CONSTITUTIONALISM, and the exercise names four features: a BICAMERAL PARLIAMENT (THE IMPERIAL DIET), the EMPEROR'S VETO AGAINST THE RESOLUTIONS OF THE DIET, the ESTABLISHMENT OF MONOCRATICALLY ORGANIZED MINISTRIES headed by a SINGLE PERSON (THE MINISTER) WHO — UNLIKE THE EMPEROR — WAS POLITICALLY ACCOUNTABLE. In 1848 the SUPREME COURT (OGH) was also established. WHAT FOLLOWED: THE BOURGEOISIE WAS OPPOSED, UNREST BROKE OUT AND THE EMPEROR PROMISED A NEW CONSTITUTION — the KREMSIER DRAFT arose, which the exercise calls HIGH CONSTITUTIONALISM and which NEVER CAME INTO FORCE.

cards.q: What did the Pillersdorf Constitution introduce and whom did it not cover?
cards.a: On 25 April 1848 it gave Austria its FIRST CONSTITUTION IN THE FORMAL SENSE and turned CISLEITHANIA INTO A CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY — but LOMBARDY-VENETIA AND HUNGARY WERE EXCLUDED FROM ITS SCOPE. Features of early constitutionalism: a BICAMERAL IMPERIAL DIET, the EMPEROR'S VETO, MONOCRATIC MINISTRIES with a POLITICALLY ACCOUNTABLE MINISTER. The same year the SUPREME COURT (OGH) was established.

cards.a: THE BOURGEOISIE WAS OPPOSED, UNREST BROKE OUT and the emperor promised a new constitution — the KREMSIER DRAFT arose, called HIGH CONSTITUTIONALISM (the sovereignty of the people), which however NEVER CAME INTO FORCE.

slides.title: Countersignature: an idea that did not work in practice
slides.text: To ministerial responsibility the exercise class adds a sentence you would not find in the textbook and which is the best part of the whole answer. THE MECHANISM: A MINISTER COULD BE CALLED TO ACCOUNT FOR A BREACH OF THE LAW — prosecuted before the STATE COURT. THE RULER HIMSELF REMAINED UNACCOUNTABLE FOR HIS CONDUCT, but EVERY ACT OF HIS HAD TO BE COUNTERSIGNED BY A MINISTER, WHO THEREBY ASSUMED LEGAL RESPONSIBILITY. AND NOW THE POINT: THE IDEA BEHIND IT WAS THAT THE MINISTER WOULD REFUSE TO SIGN UNLAWFUL ACTS OF THE RULER — IN PRACTICE, HOWEVER, THIS DID NOT WORK. It is a fine example of an institution logically perfect and politically toothless: a minister appointed and dismissed by the ruler will hardly refuse to sign what the ruler wants. That is precisely why the next step in constitutional development is the POLITICAL ACCOUNTABILITY OF THE GOVERNMENT TO PARLIAMENT, not to the ruler.

cards.q: What was the idea behind countersignature and why did it not work?
cards.a: The idea was that THE MINISTER WOULD REFUSE TO SIGN UNLAWFUL ACTS OF THE RULER, because by signing he assumed LEGAL RESPONSIBILITY (prosecution before the STATE COURT). IN PRACTICE, HOWEVER, IT DID NOT WORK — a minister appointed and dismissed by the ruler will hardly refuse to sign what the ruler wants. Hence the next step: the POLITICAL ACCOUNTABILITY OF THE GOVERNMENT TO PARLIAMENT, not to the ruler.

slides.title: Absolute and suspensive veto
slides.text: A distinction the exam asks about directly, and one where the Austrian answer is unambiguous. LEGISLATION WAS EXERCISED JOINTLY BY PARLIAMENT (THE IMPERIAL DIET) AND THE RULER; THE RULER HAD TO SIGN EVERY BILL BEFORE IT COULD BECOME LAW. AN ABSOLUTE VETO MEANS THAT NO BILL CAN BECOME LAW AGAINST THE RULER'S WILL. A SUSPENSIVE VETO MEANS THAT THE RULER CANNOT PREVENT A STATUTE FROM COMING INTO FORCE BUT ONLY DELAY IT. And the Austrian answer: IN AUSTRIA FROM 1848 TO 1918 THE VETO WAS ALWAYS ABSOLUTE. There was therefore no period in which the ruler's will could be overridden — and that in itself is a measure of how far Austrian constitutionalism reached.

cards.q: What is the difference between an absolute and a suspensive veto, and which applied in Austria?
cards.a: ABSOLUTE VETO: NO BILL CAN BECOME LAW AGAINST THE RULER'S WILL. SUSPENSIVE VETO: the ruler cannot PREVENT a statute from coming into force, only DELAY it. IN AUSTRIA FROM 1848 TO 1918 THE VETO WAS ALWAYS ABSOLUTE.

slides.title: The Rechtsstaat and the two judicial systems
slides.text: To the Rechtsstaat the exercise class gives three features and one comparison that is often asked about. THE FEATURES: (1) FOR EVERY KIND OF INTERFERENCE THERE IS A COURT BEFORE WHICH AN EFFECTIVE COMPLAINT CAN BE BROUGHT. (2) THE COURT IS INDEPENDENT AND THE JUDGES ARE SPECIALLY PROTECTED IN THAT THEY CANNOT BE ARBITRARILY REMOVED OR TRANSFERRED TO ANOTHER POST — these are, incidentally, still today the two classic guarantees of judicial independence. (3) THE STATE TOO IS BOUND BY LAW IN ITS ACTIONS, WHICH MAKES ADMINISTRATIVE AND CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION NECESSARY. That last sentence is the key one: ADMINISTRATIVE AND CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION ARE NOT AN ORNAMENT BUT A NECESSARY CONSEQUENCE OF THE STATE ITSELF BEING BOUND BY LAW. A COMPARISON OF TWO MODELS: IN ENGLAND AND THE USA THERE IS A UNIFIED JUDICIAL ORGANIZATION FOR ALL KINDS OF INTERFERENCE. IN CONTINENTAL EUROPE A DISTINCTION IS DRAWN BETWEEN CIVIL AND CRIMINAL JURISDICTION ON THE ONE HAND AND ADMINISTRATIVE JURISDICTION ON THE OTHER.

cards.q: Which three features does the Rechtsstaat have according to the exercise class?
cards.a: 1) FOR EVERY KIND OF INTERFERENCE THERE IS A COURT before which an EFFECTIVE COMPLAINT can be brought. 2) THE COURT IS INDEPENDENT and the judges CANNOT BE ARBITRARILY REMOVED OR TRANSFERRED. 3) THE STATE TOO IS BOUND BY LAW, which MAKES ADMINISTRATIVE AND CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION NECESSARY — these are therefore no ornament but a NECESSARY CONSEQUENCE.

cards.q: How do the Anglo-American and the continental judicial organizations differ?
cards.a: IN ENGLAND AND THE USA THERE IS A UNIFIED JUDICIAL ORGANIZATION FOR ALL KINDS OF INTERFERENCE. IN CONTINENTAL EUROPE a distinction is drawn between CIVIL AND CRIMINAL JURISDICTION on the one hand and ADMINISTRATIVE JURISDICTION on the other.

slides.title: A timeline of constitutions and the English exception
slides.text: The exercise class gives a COMPARATIVE SERIES that is the best answer to the question 'how should the Austrian development be judged', because it is concrete. ENGLAND ALREADY IN THE 17TH CENTURY. FRANCE AND POLAND 1791 (the Polish May Constitution is a few months older than the French and is often called the first written constitution in Europe). BELGIUM 1831 — AND THE EXERCISE ADDS THAT IT IS STILL IN FORCE. THE GERMAN STATES BETWEEN 1815 AND 1848, PRUSSIA 1848. AUSTRIA 1848 (Pillersdorf, early constitutionalism; the Kremsier draft of high constitutionalism never came into force). RUSSIA ONLY IN 1907. AUSTRIA THEREFORE DEVELOPS LATE BY COMPARISON WITH OTHER EUROPEAN COUNTRIES — but not latest of all; the west and Belgium are ahead of it, Russia behind. THE ENGLISH ROAD IS DIFFERENT AND ONE MUST BE ABLE TO SAY WHY: IT HAS NO WRITTEN CONSTITUTION — THE SOURCES OF CONSTITUTIONAL LAW ARE ACTS OF PARLIAMENT, CASE LAW AND CONVENTIONS ABOUT HOW THE ORGANS OF STATE BEHAVE. The constitutional principles there DEVELOPED OVER CENTURIES and are three: CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY, THE SOVEREIGNTY OF PARLIAMENT and THE RULE OF LAW.

cards.q: Put in order when the individual countries obtained a constitution.
cards.a: ENGLAND already in the 17TH CENTURY. FRANCE AND POLAND 1791. BELGIUM 1831 — STILL IN FORCE. THE GERMAN STATES 1815–1848, PRUSSIA 1848. AUSTRIA 1848 (Pillersdorf). RUSSIA ONLY IN 1907. Austria therefore develops LATE, but not latest of all.

cards.q: Why is the English road different and what are its principles?
cards.a: IT HAS NO WRITTEN CONSTITUTION — the sources of constitutional law are ACTS OF PARLIAMENT, CASE LAW AND CONVENTIONS about how the organs of state behave. The principles DEVELOPED OVER CENTURIES and are three: CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY, THE SOVEREIGNTY OF PARLIAMENT and THE RULE OF LAW.

slides.title: Austrian fundamental rights: three degrees of enforceability
slides.text: This is the best answer to the question about Austrian fundamental rights, because the exercise class structures it by ENFORCEABILITY, not by dates. (1) THE PILLERSDORF CONSTITUTION 1848 — merely 'STAATSZIELBESTIMMUNGEN', that is, STATE OBJECTIVES, WHICH ARE NOT ENFORCEABLE. They are instructions to the state, not claims of the citizen. (2) THE KREMSIER DRAFT 1849 — SUBJECTIVE AND ENFORCEABLE RIGHTS; the most modern point of the whole century, and it never came into force. (3) THE BASIC LAW (STAATSGRUNDGESETZ) 1867 — SUBJECTIVE RIGHTS WITH WEAK ENFORCEABILITY. And the exercise explains exactly where the weakness lies: although fundamental rights could be invoked before the IMPERIAL COURT (REICHSGERICHT), THE DECISION DID NOT LEAD TO ANNULMENT BUT WAS MERELY DECLARATORY, AND THE ADMINISTRATIVE AUTHORITIES WERE THEREFORE NOT BOUND BY IT. The court could say that a right had been violated — and nothing changed. In addition, JUDICIAL REVIEW OF THE CONSTITUTIONALITY OF STATUTES WAS NOT YET POSSIBLE. IN 1876 THE ADMINISTRATIVE COURT WAS ESTABLISHED, which could protect even subjective rights guaranteed not in the constitution but, say, in an ordinary statute, AND HAD THE POWER TO QUASH UNLAWFUL ADMINISTRATIVE ACTS — a power the Imperial Court did not have.

terms.def: A state objective — an instruction to the state, not an enforceable claim of the citizen.

cards.q: Which three degrees of enforceability did Austrian fundamental rights have?
cards.a: 1) PILLERSDORF 1848 — merely 'STAATSZIELBESTIMMUNGEN', STATE OBJECTIVES, NOT ENFORCEABLE (instructions to the state, not claims of the citizen). 2) THE KREMSIER DRAFT 1849 — SUBJECTIVE AND ENFORCEABLE RIGHTS, the most modern point of the century, never in force. 3) THE BASIC LAW 1867 — SUBJECTIVE RIGHTS WITH WEAK ENFORCEABILITY.

cards.q: Where exactly did the weak enforceability of the rights under the 1867 law lie?
cards.a: They could be invoked before the IMPERIAL COURT, but THE DECISION DID NOT LEAD TO ANNULMENT — IT WAS MERELY DECLARATORY, AND THE ADMINISTRATIVE AUTHORITIES WERE NOT BOUND BY IT: the court could say a right had been violated and nothing changed. JUDICIAL REVIEW OF STATUTES WAS NOT POSSIBLE. IN 1876 the ADMINISTRATIVE COURT was established, which COULD QUASH AN UNLAWFUL ADMINISTRATIVE ACT.

slides.title: France: rights at the centre of the order, and yet unenforceable
slides.text: The French case is the best illustration that PROCLAIMING RIGHTS AND ENFORCING THEM ARE TWO DIFFERENT THINGS. WITH THE 'DÉCLARATION DES DROITS DE L'HOMME ET DU CITOYEN' (1789) FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS BECOME THE CENTRE OF THE POLITICAL ORDER. AND YET: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS IN FRANCE WERE NOT ENFORCEABLE BEFORE THE COURTS. The reason lies in the separation of powers itself: FROM 1799 THERE WAS INDEED A COUNCIL OF STATE (CONSEIL D'ÉTAT), STRICTLY SEPARATED FROM THE CIVIL COURTS PRECISELY BECAUSE OF THE SEPARATION OF POWERS, BUT IT LACKED THE CONSTITUTIONAL GUARANTEES OF A COURT. The French conception of fundamental rights is therefore POLITICAL AND ADDRESSED TO THE LEGISLATOR — rights are a command to parliament, not a claim against it. And a detail that rounds it off: THE TERMS 'RECHTSSTAAT' AND 'RULE OF LAW' ARE TRANSLATED INTO FRENCH ONLY IN THE 20TH CENTURY. THE COMPARISON OF THE THREE ROADS IS THEREFORE: THE USA — RIGHTS ENFORCEABLE BEFORE EVERY COURT AGAINST THE LEGISLATOR (from 1803); FRANCE — RIGHTS AT THE CENTRE OF THE ORDER BUT ADDRESSED TO THE LEGISLATOR AND UNENFORCEABLE; AUSTRIA — RIGHTS GRANTED FROM ABOVE, ENFORCEABLE ONLY DECLARATORILY AND AGAINST THE ADMINISTRATION, NOT AGAINST A STATUTE.

cards.q: Why were fundamental rights not judicially enforceable in France?
cards.a: Because of the SEPARATION OF POWERS: from 1799 there was indeed a COUNCIL OF STATE (CONSEIL D'ÉTAT), STRICTLY SEPARATED FROM THE CIVIL COURTS, BUT IT LACKED THE CONSTITUTIONAL GUARANTEES OF A COURT. The French conception is therefore POLITICAL AND ADDRESSED TO THE LEGISLATOR — rights are a COMMAND TO PARLIAMENT, not a claim against it. The terms 'Rechtsstaat' and 'rule of law' are translated into French ONLY IN THE 20TH CENTURY.

cards.q: Compare the three roads to the enforceability of fundamental rights.
cards.a: THE USA — RIGHTS ENFORCEABLE BEFORE EVERY COURT AGAINST THE LEGISLATOR (from 1803). FRANCE — RIGHTS AT THE CENTRE OF THE ORDER BUT ADDRESSED TO THE LEGISLATOR AND UNENFORCEABLE. AUSTRIA — RIGHTS GRANTED FROM ABOVE, ENFORCEABLE ONLY DECLARATORILY AND AGAINST THE ADMINISTRATION, NOT AGAINST A STATUTE.

slides.title: Marbury v. Madison: what actually happened in that case
slides.text: The exercise class tells the facts, and without them the decision makes no sense. THE SUPREME COURT WAS CALLED UPON IN A POLITICAL MATTER BECAUSE A SPECIAL STATUTE DECLARED IT COMPETENT. BUT THAT SPECIAL STATUTE WAS UNCONSTITUTIONAL — THE US CONSTITUTION DOES NOT PROVIDE FOR SUCH A CONFERRAL OF JURISDICTION ON THE SUPREME COURT. THE SUPREME COURT THEREFORE DECLINED ITS JURISDICTION AND SAID: 'A LAW REPUGNANT TO THE CONSTITUTION IS VOID.' From this it follows that EVERY COURT HAS THE RIGHT TO DECIDE WHETHER A STATUTE IS CONSTITUTIONAL — that is, JUDICIAL REVIEW. NOTE THE ELEGANCE, BECAUSE IT IS THE ESSENCE OF THE CASE: THE COURT APPROPRIATED AN ENORMOUS POWER PRECISELY BY RENOUNCING POWER IN THE CASE AT HAND. Nobody could appeal, because nobody lost what they wanted. THREE PROPOSITIONS FOLLOW FOR THE USA: EVERY COURT MAY DECIDE INDEPENDENTLY ON THE CONSTITUTIONALITY OF A STATUTE; AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL STATUTE IS ABSOLUTELY VOID, THAT IS, LEGALLY NON-EXISTENT; and the principle was first stated IN 1803.

cards.q: What actually happened in Marbury v. Madison?
cards.a: The Supreme Court was called upon in a POLITICAL MATTER because a SPECIAL STATUTE DECLARED IT COMPETENT — but THAT STATUTE WAS UNCONSTITUTIONAL, because the constitution does not provide for such a conferral of jurisdiction. The Court therefore DECLINED ITS JURISDICTION with the words that 'A LAW REPUGNANT TO THE CONSTITUTION IS VOID'.

cards.q: Where does the elegance of Marbury v. Madison lie?
cards.a: THE COURT APPROPRIATED AN ENORMOUS POWER PRECISELY BY RENOUNCING POWER IN THE CASE AT HAND — nobody could appeal, because nobody lost what they wanted. For the USA it follows that EVERY COURT may decide independently on the constitutionality of a statute and that AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL STATUTE IS ABSOLUTELY VOID, that is, LEGALLY NON-EXISTENT.

slides.title: How far behind Europe was in 1803
slides.text: This comparison is the strongest sentence of the whole section and is worth having ready. WHEN THE DECISION OF THE US SUPREME COURT WAS HANDED DOWN IN 1803, MOST EUROPEAN COUNTRIES — APART FROM FRANCE AND ENGLAND — WERE STILL IN THE ERA OF (ENLIGHTENED) ABSOLUTISM, THAT IS, WITHOUT A CONSTITUTION. It was therefore not that judicial review was missing; there was nothing to review. And the Austrian part, which the exercise stresses with an exclamation mark: UNDER THE AUSTRIAN CONSTITUTION OF 1867, THAT IS, THE BASIC LAWS THAT APPLIED UNTIL 1918, AUSTRIAN COURTS WERE NOT PERMITTED TO REVIEW CONSTITUTIONALITY. ONLY WITH THE AUSTRIAN CONSTITUTION OF 1920 (B-VG) DID JUDICIAL REVIEW BECOME POSSIBLE. Between Marbury and the Austrian constitutional court there lie ONE HUNDRED AND SEVENTEEN YEARS — and that figure closes an answer on comparison better than any assessment.

cards.q: What state was Europe in in 1803, when Marbury v. Madison was decided?
cards.a: MOST EUROPEAN COUNTRIES — APART FROM FRANCE AND ENGLAND — WERE STILL IN THE ERA OF (ENLIGHTENED) ABSOLUTISM, THAT IS, WITHOUT A CONSTITUTION. It was therefore not that review was missing; THERE WAS NOTHING TO REVIEW.

cards.q: When did judicial review become possible in Austria, and what interval is that?
cards.a: ONLY WITH THE CONSTITUTION OF 1920 (B-VG). Under the basic laws of 1867, which applied UNTIL 1918, AUSTRIAN COURTS WERE NOT PERMITTED TO REVIEW CONSTITUTIONALITY. Between Marbury (1803) and the Austrian constitutional court there lie ONE HUNDRED AND SEVENTEEN YEARS.
